tagline.text: A small island off Sagay where a boardwalk winds through a community-protected mangrove forest

location.label: Location
location.text: Suyac, Barangay Taba-ao, Sagay City, Negros Occidental

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱500~1,500 (boat charter, entrance fee and lunch included, before splitting among the group)

children.text: Suyac Island is a small island inside the Sagay Marine Reserve in northern Negros, and its mangrove eco-park is run by a local community group. You can walk a wooden boardwalk through old pagatpat mangroves, kayak and swim at high tide, and enjoy a local seafood lunch.

Suyac Island is a small island floating off Barangay Taba-ao in Sagay City, at the northern tip of Negros Island. It lies inside the Sagay Marine Reserve. The island covers roughly 1.8 hectares and is ringed by about 4 hectares of mangrove forest. True to the island's name, the mangroves here are dominated by Sonneratia alba, known locally as pagatpat.

The eco-park is run not by an outside operator but by a community group, the Suyac Island Eco-Tourism Association (SIETAS). According to published accounts, 60% of the income goes to the community and 40% to facility upkeep, and there is a cap on daily visitors. It is a case where tourism income gives people a reason to protect the forest, and it has been recognized, among other things, with an ASEAN community-based tourism award.

The mood is nothing like a glossy resort island. You stroll the boardwalk through the forest, rest in a cottage, and paddle a kayak when the tide comes in, and that is about it. In return it is quiet and uncrowded, and a lunch prepared by the villagers, such as kinilaw (Filipino-style ceviche), is a real highlight. Many visitors combine it with Carbin Reef, which lies within the same reserve, as a day trip. After a day on the island, the explanation that mangroves act as nurseries for marine life and as a natural sea barrier for the coast really sinks in. For photos, the late morning, when the water is high, shows the green of the forest and the color of the sea at their best.
Sagay is a city on the northern coast of Negros, about
84km

from Bacolod. Suyac can only be reached by boat from the Sagay port, so it feels more like a village outing than a typical tourist site. The Sagay Marine Reserve is a large protected area of about 32,000 hectares, and both Suyac and Carbin Reef are part of it. On arrival you are briefed on conservation rules, and daily visitor numbers are reportedly managed at around 100. Most Negros itineraries center on Bacolod's food scene and ruins and the dive towns in the south, but heading north brings you to quiet seas and island villages. It can be done in a day from Bacolod, so even travelers short on time need only set aside half a day.

A wooden boardwalk runs into the island, so you can walk through the forest without getting your shoes wet. You can see the tangled roots and the shade up close, which makes it a good place to bring children. The boardwalk is not long, and you can walk all the way around in about
20–30 minutes
even at a slow pace. You can look at roots rising into the air up close, and crabs and small fish moving across the exposed mud at low tide are easy to spot.

The island still has old pagatpat mangroves. A sign at the entrance says Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) damaged some of the old trees, so ask the villagers to tell you how the forest has protected the community from storms. Because mangroves reduce wave energy and prevent coastal erosion, comparing them with coasts where the forest has disappeared makes it easy to understand why this island is part of the reserve.

blocks.title: Kayak and paddle tours at high tide

children.text: At high tide, when the water is at its highest, you can kayak through the channels between the mangroves. Visitors report seeing birds and fruit bats. Tours do not run at low tide, so check the timing in advance. The paddle tour has been listed at about ₱300 per person, and if you arrive when the water is low you may have to wait a few hours, so it works well to have lunch and a walk first and then paddle when the water rises.

You can swim in designated areas along the edge of the island, and at high tide it is said you can also get into the water inside the forest. There are no lifeguards, so wear a life vest and check the tide. The bottom is not fine sand but the grayish, muddy feel typical of mangrove shores, so think of it as a quick dip rather than a beach for water play.

You can eat local seafood dishes on the island, including kinilaw. If you plan to eat there, tell the staff and order before your visit. Group packages can include rice, fruit and drinks in one go, which is convenient for groups who do not want to organize their own meal.
Visitors mention seeing birds such as kingfishers. Walking quietly in the early hours improves your chances.

blocks.title: A day trip combined with Carbin Reef

children.text: Suyac and Carbin Reef are only a
10–15 minutes
boat ride apart. It is a popular pairing for travelers who want snorkeling and a mangrove forest in one trip.

items.title: Half-day route
items.subtitle: From Old Sagay Port to Suyac Island

children.text: Arrive at Old Sagay Port from Sagay City, pay the terminal fee and register as a visitor. If you have not booked in advance, check with the Sagay City tourism office.
Take a boat to Suyac Island. It is said to take about
15–20 minutes
from the port. Agree on a return time with the boatman.
On the island, listen to the house rules from a village guide and walk the boardwalk through the mangrove forest.
If the tide is high, take a kayak or paddle tour or swim in the designated area.
Rent a cottage and have a local lunch prepared by the villagers.
Take the boat back to Old Sagay Port.
If you also want to visit Carbin Reef, book the boat for both at once, and since entry numbers at both places are limited, plan your schedule early.

items.title: Full-day route
items.subtitle: Carbin Reef and Suyac Island in one trip

children.text: Take a bus or van to Sagay from Bacolod's north terminal. The distance is about
84km
and the trip takes
2–3 hours
, so leave early to catch a boat in the morning.
Take a tricycle from Sagay City to Old Sagay Port, pay the terminal fee and register as a visitor.
Stop first at Carbin Reef by boat and go snorkeling. It takes about
15 minutes
from the port.
Move from Carbin Reef to Suyac Island. It is about
10–15 minutes
by boat.
Have the lunch the villagers prepare on Suyac Island and rest in a cottage.
Time your visit to the high tide to kayak or walk the boardwalk, and take photos.
Take the boat back to Old Sagay Port.
Have a snack in Sagay City and head back to Bacolod before the last bus.
The order may change depending on the tide and boat operations, so agree on the exact plan with the boatman in the morning.
There are direct flights from Manila to Bacolod-Silay Airport (BCD). The flight takes about
1 hour 15 minutes
From the airport, go into Bacolod and take a Sagay-bound bus from the north bus terminal.
Bacolod to Sagay takes about
2–3 hours
by bus or van and the distance is about
84km
. Both ordinary and air-conditioned buses run, so check locally.
From the Sagay city bus terminal, take a tricycle to Old Sagay Port.
At the port, pay the terminal fee, register and board a boat to the island. It takes about
15–20 minutes
from the port.
Boat charter rates vary by boat size and route, so check locally.
Booking the boat through the Sagay boat operators' association is the arrangement recommended in guides.
The dry season from November to May is the most reliable. The sea is calm, which makes boat rides easier, and the skies are clear, so the mangrove forest photographs well.
Kayaking and swimming inside the forest are possible only at high tide. Check the high-tide time for your visit date and arrive to match it.

In the rainy season, typhoons and rough seas often cancel boats, so check the weather and boat operations right before you travel. If the tide does not suit the day, you may not be able to kayak, so we recommend planning with a tide table.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.
The island is said to have no overnight accommodation, so visit as a day trip. It is common to stay in Sagay City or Bacolod and head to the port early in the morning.

Lunch centers on dishes the villagers prepare on the island. Seafood such as kinilaw is famous, and if you plan to eat there, let them know before your visit. Bringing outside food may carry a separate fee, so check.

Sagay has lodging for visitors to the marine reserve, and a 2017 source described a lodging called Balay Kauswagan as offering everything from dormitory beds to family rooms. Check locally whether it still operates and what it charges. In Sagay City there is also a children's museum, Museo Sang Bata sa Negros, which is suggested as a good morning stop.

Around Sagay port you can easily find restaurants and snack shops, so if you do not plan to eat on the island, you can eat on the way back. Visitors report that a small fee may be charged for bringing outside food onto the island.
Visitor numbers are limited, so contact the Sagay City tourism office in advance to reserve.
Kayaking and swimming inside the forest are possible only at high tide, so schedule your arrival around the tide.
Bring drinking water, sunscreen, a hat and swimwear, and carry a power bank for charging.
Take your trash back with you, and do not break or touch mangrove roots and branches.
If you visit Carbin Reef too, one boat trip covers both places and saves money.
Be sure to follow the island rules that the guides explain before you start.
Fees and operations change often, so check the latest announcements before you leave.
To do it in a day from Bacolod, take the first bus.
Check the tourism office's contact details locally for the latest, and for group bookings ask at least a week in advance.
There are no lifeguards on the island and swimming depends heavily on the tide, so wear a life vest and swim only in designated areas.
Boats may not run on days with rough seas, so leave some slack in your schedule.
Guides say smoking is restricted outside designated spots and dogs are not allowed on the island.
Fee information differs by source, so confirm the exact amounts on site.
Some times of day have little shade, so beware of heat stroke.
Shade and restrooms are basic, so children and older travelers should bring water and a hat.
About
10–15 minutes
from Suyac by boat, a coral reef in the Sagay Marine Reserve where you can snorkel.
The central city of Negros Occidental, where Sagay-bound buses depart, and where direct flights from Manila land. It is a good place to spend a day before or after your trip and try the local food.
A historic town near Bacolod, easy to stop at while heading north.
Another island getaway on the northern coast of Negros.
